source.title: CodeGen2: Lessons for Training LLMs on Programming and Natural Languages
source.authors: E. Nijkamp; Hiroaki Hayashi; Cai-Ming Xiong; S. Savarese; Ying-Bo Zhou

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no evident garbling or cutoff.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream task performance across sizes of code language models and training-token budgets, extending scaling-related observations to programming models. It does not fit or test held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Rows record the reported HumanEval and HumanEval-Infill scores across CodeGen2.0 sizes, plus HumanEval pass@k results across the token budgets in Table 3. The paper does not report held-out pretraining-loss curves, small-run extrapolations, compute-optimal allocations, or power-law fits. Figure 1 reports downstream metrics over training steps and data mixtures; its findings compare data-mixture conditions, not loss scaling or prediction from model scale, so those results are not included as rows for the claim versions.
record.test_reason: Weak test of V6 only. CodeGen2.0 is trained with one recipe at 1B, 3.7B, 7B and 16B and scored on HumanEval and HumanEval-Infill, so it shows downstream scores across model size in code models. This is a model-release table, not a scaling analysis: no loss curves, no fit and no prediction. Scaling laws appear only as motivation in the introduction.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but the paper's conclusions are five design lessons. Prefix-LM gives no measurable benefit; infill is not a free lunch; a simple CLM plus within-file span-corruption mixture suffices; NL/PL data mixing looks promising; multi-epoch training is strongly effective (CodeGen2.5). Scaling laws are invoked only as motivation, and no scaling conclusion is drawn.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates code-model sizes and training-token regimes using downstream task scores; it does not fit held-out-loss scaling laws or optimize a fixed-compute parameter/token split.
record.method_sensitivity: Training data, training-token budget, and model size vary across the reported comparisons; Table 3 also reports different pass@k sampling temperatures.

fits_no_version.finding: Training a 7B model for 5 epochs (1.4T tokens) on repeated StarCoderData raises HumanEval pass@1 from 18.83 to 28.36 and pass@100 from 50.41 to 75.15, versus the 400B-token CodeGen2.0-7B. The comparison is confounded by dataset and LR schedule.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-epoch training on repeated code data keeps improving downstream code-synthesis performance beyond the point of new data.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant benchmark scores. Downstream benchmark results do not measure pretraining loss or establish power-law fit or extrapolation. The CodeGen2.0 versus CodeGen2.5 comparison changes multiple training factors, and the authors explicitly leave their individual contributions unresolved.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results left out. Figure 1's training-step and data-mixture comparisons are not recorded as rows because they do not test the versions' scale-to-performance predictability claim.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss across parameters, tokens or compute, and no power-law fit.
No fits on small runs and no extrapolation.
No depth or width comparison at fixed parameter count. The Prefix-LM vs causal-decoder comparison uses downstream scores, not loss shape.
Multi-epoch (repeated-data) training is run, but no loss and no power-law form is measured.
Predictability: no fitted relation of downstream score to scale or to pretraining loss. Token-budget scaling is not isolated from other changes.
No fitting choices or curve bends are examined.

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is incidental: a model-family results table, not a scaling study. Baselines are the smaller model sizes in the same table. The InCoder 1.3B/6.7B numbers in Table 1 are baseline comparisons from another model family and are correctly left out as rows.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy measurements or power-law fits in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No fits on small runs or predictions evaluated against much larger runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count using loss.
The paper studies programming-language models, but does not test whether power-law loss forms transfer to another modality or training regime.
Reports downstream task scores across model sizes and token budgets, but does not test their predictability from pretraining loss or fit a quantitative scaling relation.
No comparison of fitting choices, loss-curve bends, or disagreement among fitted scaling laws.

relationships.condition: CodeGen2.0 size sweep (1B–16B, same recipe, 400B tokens), HumanEval and HumanEval-Infill
relationships.reason: Scores rise monotonically with size on every measure: pass@1 10.27→14.88→19.09→20.46, Infill-Single 53.41→68.74, Infill-Multi 23.41→38.88, and 7B→16B pass@k (r1–r12, r14, r15, r17, r18). Only four points, no fit, and the 16B model was unconverged.
relationships.display_finding: HumanEval pass@1 increased through 10.27, 14.88, 19.09, and 20.46, infilling scores increased from 53.41 to 68.74 and 23.41 to 38.88, and pass@k improved from 7B to 16B, although 16B remained unconverged and no predictive relationship was fitted.
